unit.title: Let the computer search: knapsack, routes, timetables

lesson.title: Timetables with CP-SAT
lesson.subtitle: Rules as lines, a solver that searches, and who gets the bad slot

video.title: Timetables with CP-SAT
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — your computer studies teacher (main character)
Mr Okafor Eze — your science teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talks to the student)

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph at a noticeboard with four club posters (chess, football, drama, coding) and a three-day grid.
scenes.animation: Posters shuffle between days; a laptop slides in.
scenes.narration: Four clubs, three afternoons, and one student who’s in three of them. Every term we argue about which club meets when. This term, let’s let a solver search.

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the Optimization track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: timetables with CP-SAT, from Google’s OR-Tools.

scenes.visual: Four club cards with a small dial (1 to 3) each; student faces linked to their clubs; a football field with a ‘busy’ tag on day 3.
scenes.animation: Dials spin; links draw; the tag drops.
scenes.narration: Each club gets a variable: its day, from one to three. Each student’s clubs must all be on different days. And the football field is busy on day three. That’s the whole model.

scenes.visual: Code typed on a card, each part lighting up as it is named.
scenes.animation: Code types itself line by line.
scenes.narration: In Python, that’s a dictionary of day variables, one all-different rule per student, and one line for the field.

scenes.visual: A grid of clubs by days: crosses stamp into impossible cells; one guess is placed and lifted.
scenes.animation: Crosses stamp; a guess wobbles and returns.
scenes.narration: The solver doesn’t try all eighty-one plans. It crosses out days that can’t work, guesses only when it’s stuck, and undoes any guess that hits a dead end. That’s propagation and search.

scenes.animation: Bars grow; the tall one keeps climbing.
scenes.narration: In the lab’s school timetable, propagation and search need eight guesses. Plain backtracking needs three hundred and eighty-nine. Add one rule, and the search needs only two.

scenes.visual: Sara’s three clubs try to fit into two remaining days; a stamp ‘No timetable’ lands.
scenes.animation: Cards jostle for two slots; the stamp drops.
scenes.narration: Sometimes the answer is INFEASIBLE, and that’s a proof, not a failure. Sara is in chess, drama and coding, so she needs three different days. Add a rule that no club meets on day three, and only two days are left. The solver proves no timetable exists.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor with a printout saying OPTIMAL. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Our club model has no goal, and the solver says OPTIMAL. What does OPTIMAL mean here?

scenes.visual: The answer ‘keeps every rule’ gets a check; a thought bubble of students’ wishes floats outside the model.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops; the bubble drifts off.
scenes.narration: With no goal, OPTIMAL just means a timetable that keeps every rule. Not the fairest, and not the one students would pick. Only what you wrote down.

scenes.visual: A calendar where drama sits on the day before every holiday; then the days rotate across terms.
scenes.animation: Drama’s card slides to a new day each term.
scenes.narration: So look at who carries the cost. If drama always gets the last afternoon before the holiday, the same students always miss it. Write fairness down, as a rule like rotating days each term, and solve again.

scenes.visual: A phone with the lab: the lessons-by-periods grid, rule checkboxes, a guess counter.
scenes.animation: A finger ticks rules; the counter drops.
scenes.narration: In the app, open “Build the timetable”. Press One step to watch propagation, then Run. Tick the extra rules one at a time, and watch the guesses fall, then the proof.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph points at a laptop showing INFEASIBLE. Three answer cards appear.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Your club model says INFEASIBLE. What should you do first?

scenes.visual: The answer card gets the check; four summary lines and a takeaway bar.
scenes.animation: Lines tick in; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.narration: Find the rules that clash, and ask the people involved which one can bend. Remember: a variable for each choice, a line for each rule, and the solver crosses out and searches. INFEASIBLE is a proof. And OPTIMAL only keeps the rules you wrote.

scenes.visual: A student with a phone and a weekly planner; chores and subjects as cards on a grid.
scenes.animation: Cards settle into days; one rotates.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: model your study week, or your family’s chores, with the same few lines. Who gets the worst slot? Add a rule to share it, and solve again.

checkpoints.prompt: The club model has no goal, and the solver says OPTIMAL. What does that mean?

options.text: It found a timetable that keeps every rule
It found the best timetable for everyone

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — with no goal, OPTIMAL means every rule you wrote is kept. Nothing more.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — with no goal there is no ‘best’: OPTIMAL means a timetable that keeps every rule you wrote.

checkpoints.prompt: Your club model says INFEASIBLE. What should you do first?

options.text: Run it again: it might work next time
Find which rules clash, and decide with people which can bend

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — INFEASIBLE proves the rules clash. Find the clash and agree which rule bends.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — INFEASIBLE is a proof, so running again changes nothing, and deleting rules at random may drop one that matters. Find the clash and decide together.
